title: The Mole Concept: Counting Particles by Weighing

questions.question: Avogadro's number is:
questions.rationale: One mole contains 6.022 × 10²³ particles — the count of atoms in exactly 12 g of carbon-12.

questions.question: The molar mass of carbon dioxide is:
questions.rationale: M(CO₂) = 12 + 2(16) = 44 g/mol, so 44 g of CO₂ is exactly one mole.

questions.question: How many moles are in 18 g of water (M = 18 g/mol)?
questions.rationale: n = m/M = 18/18 = 1 mol — which holds 6.022 × 10²³ molecules.

questions.question: At STP, one mole of any ideal gas occupies:
questions.rationale: Molar volume at 273 K and 1 atm is 22.4 L per mole, regardless of the gas.

questions.question: 5.85 g of NaCl (M = 58.5 g/mol) dissolved to make 500 mL of solution gives a molarity of:
The number of molecules in 11.2 L of a gas at STP is:
questions.rationale: 11.2 L is half of 22.4 L, so half a mole — 0.5 × 6.022 × 10²³ = 3.011 × 10²³ molecules.

questions.question: The empirical formula of glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆) is:
questions.rationale: Dividing all subscripts by 6 gives the simplest whole-number ratio, CH₂O.

questions.question: Burning 4 g of hydrogen in 32 g of oxygen produces how much water?
questions.rationale: Mass is conserved: 4 g + 32 g = 36 g of water, matching 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O (2 mol).

questions.question: If 10 g of H₂ is mixed with 32 g of O₂, the limiting reagent is:
questions.rationale: 10 g of H₂ is 5 mol, needing 2.5 mol (80 g) of O₂; only 1 mol (32 g) is present, so oxygen caps the yield.

questions.question: The mass percentage of hydrogen in water is about:
questions.rationale: 2/18 = 11.1% hydrogen by mass; oxygen makes up the remaining 88.9%.
